What I’ve already done

• Cursor AI for 2+ years as primary IDE for generate / refine / explain.

• Four years of non-page-builder WordPress builds (ACF Pro Gutenberg blocks as the main pattern).
• On the build above:
  ◦ Figma MCP + project rules/skills for ACF block creation, CSS conventions, forms, and validation
  ◦ Agent drafts against the theme’s block system
  ◦ I review diffs, responsive behavior, and ship via staging
• A repeatable system (so I don’t re-teach the project every session):
  ◦ Standing project instructions - stack, structure, and house style
  ◦ Always-on rules - CSS/markup conventions, security, no-bloat limits
  ◦ On-demand skills - ACF block scaffold, CPT wiring, form + validation setup, Figma section mapping
  ◦ Reference patterns - existing blocks the agent copies instead of inventing
  ◦ Small checks before ship - responsive, fields save/render, forms submit, no PHP notices
• Outcome: faster builds without pasting AI straight to production.

────────────────────────────────────────
How I work (high level)
────────────────────────────────────────
• Start from the task + the project’s standing conventions (not a blank chat).
• Pull design context from Figma MCP (and project specs when present); map to existing blocks or scaffold a new ACF section.
• Prompt for a concrete change; let the agent draft against those conventions.
• Review the diff for:
  ◦ Security
  ◦ Design fidelity
  ◦ Responsive behavior
  ◦ Bloat
• Run checks; fix failures; ship.
• When the same mistake shows up twice, I fix the system (rule / skill / check), not only the file.

**WordPress build + Cursor / AI**  
Jonathan A. Rapusas  
Senior WordPress Developer Application

Agency client work sits under NDA. No live URLs, localhost, client repos, Figma files, or screenshots of those builds. I don't screen-share client projects.

What follows is a written description of one typical Figma → custom WordPress build - stack, blocks, content model - with no client files or identity. Then how I use Cursor / AI day to day.

On request: an agency recommendation. Visual proof of fit: Studio1's paid 4-week trial.

---

## Part 1 - How a typical build runs

Usual delivery path:

1. Approved Figma plus brand and functionality specs  
2. Gantt / schedule  
3. Map sections to WordPress  
4. Staging  
5. Feedback  
6. Production  
7. Handoff / maintenance  

### Multi-page marketing site from Figma (custom theme)

Recent full build: a site redesign from Figma and written functionality specs.

**Handoff.** Figma frames become design tokens and a section map, then WordPress. Sometimes I go straight to theme work. Sometimes I cut a short HTML prototype first when stakeholders need something clickable before the CMS layer.

**Stack.** Custom PHP theme. ACF Pro Gutenberg section blocks. ACF JSON field groups. Gravity Forms. Staging, then production.

**Site shape.** Homepage sections, plus flexible inner pages built from the same block library. Sitewide header, nav, footer, and search. Contact with a map. Blog.

**Blocks shipped** (examples of the vocabulary, not a full list):

- Masthead / hero  
- Half-and-half media / text  
- Text + stats  
- Image buttons / cards  
- Image gallery slider  
- History timeline  
- Leadership / team grid  
- Testimonials  
- CTA banner  
- Icon cards  
- WYSIWYG  
- Contact form  

**Content model.** Custom post types (projects, team, testimonials, galleries, and the like) feed the blocks. Options-driven block presets let editors reuse section content across pages instead of rebuilding the same hero every time.

**The pattern I care about.** One shared section system. New pages assemble existing blocks. I don't want a one-off template for every new page.

---

## Part 2 - How I use Cursor / AI

Cursor is my daily AI agent IDE. Same class of tool as Claude for this work: multi-file agents against standing project conventions, then I review and ship.

I'm on Composer 2.5 today. If Studio1 standardizes on Claude, the same rules, skills, and Figma MCP workflow move over. That isn't a restart from chat history.

AI drafts. I own quality. AI never deploys itself.

I walked my agency team through the principles here:  
https://www.jorap.com/blog/consistent-ai-output-wordpress-builds/

### What I've already done

- Cursor as my primary IDE for generate / refine / explain for 2+ years  
- About a year of HTML → WordPress with AI  
- About a year of Figma prototypes → WordPress with AI through Figma MCP (needs a Figma account with Dev Mode)  
- Four years of non-page-builder WordPress builds, with ACF Pro Gutenberg blocks as the main pattern  

On the build above: Figma MCP plus project rules and skills for ACF block creation, CSS conventions, forms, and validation. The agent drafts against the theme's block system. I review the diffs and responsive behavior, then ship through staging.

I keep a repeatable system so I don't re-teach the project every session:

- Standing project instructions - stack, structure, house style  
- Always-on rules - CSS/markup conventions, security, no-bloat limits  
- On-demand skills - ACF block scaffold, CPT wiring, form + validation setup, Figma section mapping  
- Reference patterns - existing blocks the agent copies instead of inventing  
- Small checks before ship - responsive, fields save and render, forms submit, no PHP notices  

Outcome: faster builds without pasting AI straight to production.

### How I work (high level)

I start from the task and the project's standing conventions - not a blank chat.

I pull design context from Figma MCP (and project specs when they're there), then map to an existing block or scaffold a new ACF section.

I prompt for a concrete change and let the agent draft against those conventions.

I review the diff for security, design fidelity, responsive behavior, and bloat.

I run checks, fix failures, and ship.

When the same mistake shows up twice, I fix the system (rule, skill, or check) - not only the file.

### Fit for Studio1

I'm already AI-first on Figma → WordPress (Cursor + Figma MCP). I'm not learning that on the job.

Recent production proof: a full custom-theme redesign with a reusable ACF Gutenberg section library.

Cursor covers the Claude-class workflow today. A house-tool swap to Claude keeps the rules and skills intact.

I think in systems: improve the workflow when it drifts, instead of chasing one-off hero prompts.

### Also available

Happy to answer questions about the Figma → WordPress / AI process. Agency professional recommendation on request.

The user is asking whether "vibe coding" can be defined as someone who only uses prompts. This likely relates to their Studio1 application, possibly to distinguish their approach from pure prompt-only methods.

"Vibe coding" originally meant accepting AI-generated code based on vibes and prompts without careful review. The user's "prompts only" framing is a useful shorthand for their own method, but it oversimplifies the original concept.

That framing works well for their letter. It is not strictly accurate though. Vibe coding is more like prompting until it feels right and shipping without deep review. The anti-pattern contrast remains valid.

_**Agent (auto-smart)**_

Mostly yes - for your letter that contrast works.

Public meaning (Karpathy-ish): chat until it “feels right,” accept code on vibes, light review. Prompt-only is the usual shape of that. Not always *only* prompts - sometimes people paste files - but no standing rules, skills, or hard checks.

Your contrast stays clean:

- **Vibe coding:** blank chat → prompts → ship what looks good  
- **You:** standing conventions → agent drafts → you review + checks → ship  

If you name it, one plain line beats a definition dump:

> I'm not doing vibe coding - blank chat and prompts until it looks right. I keep rules, skills, and checks so the next session matches the last one.

Skip “vibe coding” entirely if the reader might hear slang as unserious. Say “prompt-only / no project rules” instead. Same point, safer for a hiring note.
